item.title: China's holiday consumption market posts steady growth
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
Tourists interact with actors at Yangliuqing ancient town in Tianjin, north China, Oct. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Ran)
BEIJING, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Consumer spending across China is holding steady midway through the seven-day National Day holiday, with early data pointing to stable growth that reflects the economy's underlying vitality.
In the first three days of the holiday from Oct. 1 to 3, foot traffic and revenue at 78 major shopping streets and commercial districts monitored by the Ministry of Commerce rose 3.4 percent and 5.3 percent year on year, respectively.
Notably, the government's consumer goods trade-in program drove 19.63 billion yuan (about 2.91 billion U.S. dollars) in sales over the same period, benefiting 3.48 million consumers.
In breakdown, the program drove trade-ins of 46,000 vehicles, generating 7.45 billion yuan in new car sales, along with 1.51 million home appliances worth 6.5 billion yuan and 1.71 million digital and smart devices worth 4.9 billion yuan.
The National Day holiday has long been one of China's peak periods for travel, tourism and spending. Authorities had projected 2.13 billion cross-regional passenger trips in total over the seven days, averaging 300 million a day.
Previous data have suggested demand remains strong as railway passenger trips on Oct. 1 alone reached 25.2 million, a single-day record.
To meet surging demand, China has added train services on busy routes and waived highway tolls for private cars during the holiday.
Moreover, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism launched a month-long national tourism promotion campaign in late September.
Local governments are hosting more than 20,000 events spanning scenic trips, autumn outings, red tourism, study tours, night activities and local food to boost diverse premium tourism offerings, while also handing out some 310 million yuan in consumer vouchers and subsidies over the month as a way to spur tourism consumption.

item.title: Ambassador Xie Feng and Madame Wang Dan Attended "ShanghaiEye Night" Events
item.description:

Chinese Ambassador to the U.S. Xie Feng highlighted the importance of cultural exchange and people-to-people ties at the “Future Resonance — ShanghaiEye Night” event in Washington, D.C.
Speaking at the October 3 gathering, Xie said cultural exchanges can help bridge differences, deepen mutual understanding and strengthen ties between China and the United States. He also called on business and community leaders to support more cooperation between the two countries.
The ambassador and his wife, Madame Wang Dan, were invited to the event as part of the “Shanghai Let’s Meet” city promotion initiative, which brought together government, business and community representatives and recognized individuals and organizations for their contributions to China-U.S. friendship.

item.title: Lula, Flavio Bolsonaro head to runoff in Brazil presidential election
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
BRASILIA, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Brazil's presidential election will head to a runoff on Oct. 25 after no candidate secured a majority of valid votes in the first round, official results showed Sunday.
According to results released by the Superior Electoral Court, with over 99 percent of the ballots counted, Flavio Bolsonaro, presidential candidate of Brazil's Liberal Party, garnered about 47 percent of valid votes. Incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party came in second with about 45 percent.

item.title: China upholds principles, promotes dialogue at G20 trade ministers' meeting: commerce ministry
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
BEIJING, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- China played an active role in promoting dialogue and cooperation with other G20 members while upholding principles during the recent G20 trade ministers' meeting, the country's Ministry of Commerce said on Sunday.
The ministry spokesperson made the remarks in response to a media question about the meeting, which was held on Sept. 30 and Oct. 1 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, the United States.
Members exchanged views on issues proposed by the U.S. G20 presidency, including opposing the weaponization of food, addressing overcapacity, eliminating forced labor, and adjusting the Most-Favored-Nation (MFN) principle.
Members reached a joint statement opposing the weaponization of food, while no outcome documents were issued on the remaining matters, according to the ministry.
During the meeting, the Chinese side consistently upheld an attitude of openness and cooperation, constructively participated in discussions and maintained close communication with other members, fully playing its role in promoting dialogue and cooperation, said the spokesperson.
At the same time, China adhered to its principles, resolutely safeguarded the common interests of China and other developing countries, and worked to promote unity and cooperation within the G20, the ministry added.
Regarding the food issue, many emerging market and developing members, including China, put forward the view that food-importing and food-exporting countries should jointly safeguard the stability of food supply chains, and that all parties have the right to take measures for domestic public policy objectives and to safeguard food security, the spokesperson said.
The presidency gave positive consideration to these views, which were also fully reflected in the joint statement, the spokesperson said, adding that the outcome was the result of consensus-building and the joint efforts of all G20 members.
Issues such as overcapacity and forced labor were highly controversial from the outset, said the ministry. The ministry said that at present, G20 members are generally subject to additional Section 301 tariffs under the pretext of so-called "forced labor" and are mostly targets of Section 301 investigations over the so-called "overcapacity" issue.
Against this backdrop, many members put forward different views on the issues set by the presidency, and the meeting ultimately failed to produce outcome documents on these matters, the ministry said.
The spokesperson also noted that, after the meeting, the U.S. side issued a chair's statement mentioning that it had released a statement on forced labor with two other G20 countries outside the G20 framework.
On the issue of reforming the MFN treatment principle, the vast majority of members, including China, emphasized that the principle is the cornerstone of the multilateral trading system, providing stability and predictability for global trade, and that any undermining of this principle would seriously damage the foundation of the multilateral trading system, said the ministry.
In light of the views expressed by the members, the presidency did not propose an outcome document on this topic, the ministry revealed.
Looking ahead to the G20 Leaders' Summit in December 2026, the spokesperson said that China is ready to work with the G20 presidency and all members to uphold consensus-building, and jointly contribute positive and practical economic and trade outcomes to the summit.

item.title: Over 300 artifacts, documents debut in Beijing as China marks 90th anniversary of Long March victory
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
A woman visits a themed exhibition commemorating the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March at the Military Museum of the Chinese People's Revolution during a media preview in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Yin Gang)
BEIJING, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- More than 300 artifacts and historical documents related to the Long March are being exhibited for the first time at a military museum in Beijing, offering new details about an event that helped shape the history of the 20th century.
The exhibition comes as China marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, which concluded in October 1936 when the main forces of the Red Army broke through the siege of the Kuomintang forces and reunited in northwest China.
The military odyssey of roughly 12,500 kilometers, which started in 1934, not only preserved the revolutionary forces, but also gave the Communist Party of China (CPC) a new foothold from which to grow the strength of the revolution, and a new starting point from which to carry the revolution forward to victory.
One highlight of the exhibition is a collection of manuscripts recounting battles, radio communications, daily experiences and other aspects of the journey. Some were written by the individuals themselves, while most were compiled from their oral accounts.
These manuscripts offer valuable firsthand records, while also displaying literary merit, said a guide at the Military Museum of the Chinese People's Revolution, which is hosting the themed exhibition.
Among them is a manuscript by a division commander, recounting how his unit tried to hold back enemy forces at the Xiangjiang River in late 1934.
Historical records show that the Central Red Army emerged from the campaign with just over 30,000 troops, down from more than 86,000 at the start of the Long March.
An exhibition curator at the museum said that the newly displayed materials, along with the personal belongings of those who died in battle, help broaden knowledge of what happened in key battles during the Long March. They also provide valuable source material for research into military history.
Over the past nine decades, the Long March has drawn journalists, writers and scholars from around the world to retrace its route and explore its history as a way to understand the CPC and China today.
More than a strategic military maneuver, it is widely regarded as a saga of ideals, devotion, willpower and bravery.
Another group of newly displayed artifacts offers a glimpse into how Red Army soldiers pushed the limits of human endurance in some of the most unforgiving terrain along the route.
They include a blue, single-layer coat and a simple knitted blanket used by soldiers to keep warm while crossing snow-covered mountains, as well as everyday items such as a fire-starting tool and a first-aid pouch.
According to information presented at the exhibition, the main forces of the Red Army climbed more than 20 snow-covered mountains rising above 4,000 meters during the Long March.
Thin air, deep ravines and rapidly changing weather made the journey a constant test of endurance. Some soldiers collapsed from exhaustion, while others froze to death.
Hundreds of kilometers of marshland posed another formidable challenge for the Red Army. The terrain was so treacherous that it was described as a "death trap," with hidden marshes that could swallow people and animals without warning.
Many soldiers lost their lives there. Some died of illness or starvation, while others were poisoned by wild plants they ate in a desperate bid to survive. Others simply disappeared in the marshes.
The exhibition in Beijing features newly displayed artifacts from this ordeal, including half of a belt, with the other half having been eaten by a soldier, a fishing line used by a senior officer to catch fish for food, and straw sandals reinforced with cloth that soldiers wore while crossing the marshlands.
Keith Bennett, international relations consultant and vice president of the London-based 48 Group, pointed to conviction, discipline and perseverance as enduring values of the Long March, saying they continue to inspire China's modernization and its vision of multipolarity, global cooperation and shared progress.
The spirit of the Long March, he said, remains a living force in contemporary China, guiding endeavors like poverty alleviation, rural revitalization, scientific innovation, ecological civilization and major national development goals.
The exhibition's new displays also turn to another part of the Long March story: the people who lived along the route. The objects offer a glimpse into the ties the CPC and the Red Army sought to build with local communities.
Among these items are a tablecloth that Mao Zedong gave to a member of the Miao ethnic group in Guizhou, a volleyball soldiers left behind in Sichuan, and a pair of goggles presented to a guide in Yunnan. All three provinces lie in southwest China.
Other artifacts include black ramie cloth and scissors given to people in Guizhou to show gratitude for their help, as well as a porcelain bowl presented to a family in Sichuan that took in a wounded soldier and cared for him as he recovered.
Elsbeth van Paridon, a Dutch sinologist who joined a group retracing the Long March this summer, said walking the route gave her a feeling similar to looking out over the beaches of Normandy and realizing what had happened there.
She described the objective of the Long March as "making it all about the people."
She noted that the former revolutionary sites along the route now also serve as ecological parks, becoming part of a broader tourism economy that supports local development.
"That is how you see the spirit of the Long March live on," she said.
The exhibition covers around 3,300 square meters and features 875 artifacts, including individual pieces and sets, along with 186 historical documents -- 1,061 items in all. It also features 357 photographs and charts and 73 artworks.
Carefully designed displays recreate key episodes along the Long March, from the seizure of the Luding Bridge and the battle to break through Lazikou Pass to a meeting held in Zunyi, Guizhou, in 1935.
The museum has previously staged three themed exhibitions commemorating the Long March, in 1996, 2006 and 2016.
For the first time, this year's exhibition includes English-language descriptions. It will remain on display as part of the museum's permanent exhibition.

item.title: Beyond the tourist trail: China's holiday travel takes new turns
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
Four days into China's seven-day National Day holiday, the country is still on the move, with travelers doing far more than simply ticking off landmarks.
China's railways carried 19.27 million passenger trips on Saturday alone, up 6.1% year on year, with cross-regional trips exceeding 300 million on October 3. Rail operators added overnight high-speed trains on the busiest routes, and at many stations "tourist service centers" help visitors buy attraction tickets and catch shuttle buses the moment they step off the train.
But the numbers tell only half the story. Booking data from major online travel platforms suggests a quiet shift in how Chinese people travel: longer stays, wider itineraries and experiences that go deeper than a photo stop. Multi-destination trips are on the rise – users booking flights to two or more cities grew 70%, and many now treat once-overlooked transit hubs as destinations in their own right.
Vehicles travel along the Lüyashan Scenic Highway amid vibrant autumn foliage in Ningwu County, Xinzhou City, north China's Shanxi Province, October 3, 2026. /VCG
Chasing autumn
Searches related to "autumn viewing" jumped 80% this season, and poetry-inspired leaf-peeping has put cities like Xi'an, Nanjing and Luoyang on more itineraries. One social media platform reported searches for the Greater Hinggan Mountains in China's far northeast up 490%, as travelers swap tips on where the golden birch forests and wetlands are at their peak – some posting daily "progress bars" of the changing colors, others sharing self-drive routes with mapped-out stops.
In Shilin Village, in Yuyao, east China's Zhejiang Province, autumn is something you can taste. The village grows over 18 hectares of persimmon trees yielding more than 150 tonnes of fruit a year. As the harvest ripens, residents peel persimmons for drying and hang corn, chilies and red beans from doorways and rooftops, a tradition known as "shaiqiu," or sunning the autumn harvest. Visitors can sip persimmon coffee, sample persimmon pastries and make persimmon-scented sachets. The village expects over 30,000 visitors during the holiday.
Classics are also drawing crowds. At Huaguo Mountain in Lianyungang, Jiangsu Province, legendary home of the Monkey King, performances bring "Journey to the West" to life, with young visitors making up nearly 40% of ticket sales.
Moviegoers enter a cinema to watch a film in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, October 4, 2026. /VCG
The ticket-stub economy
The holiday box office crossed 600 million yuan (about $89 million) by mid-holiday, led by domestic titles spanning comedy, mystery, romance and animation. But cinemas have become gateways to something bigger: in Shenzhen, a movie ticket stub doubles as a raffle entry for food festival perks and dining vouchers, while the Luohu MixC shopping district launched a "film + food" pilot with a fine-dining market, letting cinemas and restaurants feed customers to each other.
In Liuzhou, Guangxi, a single ticket stub unlocks discounts at more than 80 businesses – bookstores, hotels, scenic spots and the city's famed river-snail rice noodle shops.
Perhaps the most striking example is Shitanjing, a former coal mining town in Ningxia's Shizuishan. After the hit film Once Upon a Time in the Middle East was shot there, crews left most of the sets standing. Now the town moonlights as a tourist attraction between productions, with food markets and interactive performances built around the film. Nearly 60 productions have been shot in the area in recent years, spawning three film service companies and a local actors' guild, and professional studios are planned to turn its weathered industrial landscape into a lasting draw.
Customers try out Huawei Mate 90 series smartphones at a Huawei store in Shanghai, east China, as shopping malls see strong consumer activity during the National Day holiday, October 2, 2026. /VCG
Spending with support
Consumption is getting a policy tailwind. In the first three days of the holiday, duty-free shopping on the island of Hainan reached 358 million yuan, up 8.85% year on year, with 55,100 shoppers.
Nationally, 62.5 billion yuan in new funding for consumer goods trade-ins landed just before the holiday. In Tianjin, subsidies reached up to 1,500 yuan for home appliances, alongside 80 million yuan in government vouchers. In Sichuan, a personal consumer loan interest subsidy – a one-percentage-point annual discount applied automatically at repayment, with no fees – has backed over 399 billion yuan in loans benefiting 3.41 million consumers. Nationwide, more than 20,000 cultural and tourism events and 310 million yuan in vouchers are on offer this month.
The message from this Golden Week is clear: China's holidaymakers are staying longer, venturing further, and the economy is finding new ways to meet them there.

item.title: Boonson, Yu take MVP honors at 2026 Asian Games
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi (L) and Thai sprinter Puripol Boonson pose with the awards for the most valuable player (MVP) of the 20th Asian Games during the awarding ceremony at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Oct. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Hou Zhaokang)
NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Thai sprinter Puripol Boonson and Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi were named the men's and women's Most Valuable Players of the 2026 Asian Games, the Olympic Council of Asia announced Sunday.
Boonson won the men's 100m and 200m titles and took silver in the mixed 4x100m relay. The 20-year-old clocked an Asian Games record of 9.90 seconds in the 100m, becoming the only finalist to break the 10-second barrier.
"It is something that makes both my family and my country proud and happy," Boonson said. "This achievement has given me a tremendous boost in confidence. With the Los Angeles Olympics coming up, I will give my all to win a medal there."
Yu, 13, claimed three gold medals, setting an Asian record in the women's 200m individual medley and Asian Games records in the 200m butterfly and 400m individual medley.
"I will continue to train hard, push myself and work alongside young athletes across Asia to inspire more young people to love and take part in sports, especially swimming," she said.
Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi poses with the award for the most valuable player (MVP) of the 20th Asian Games during the awarding ceremony at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Oct. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Hou Zhaokang)
Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi (2nd L) and Thai sprinter Puripol Boonson (2nd R), the most valuable players (MVP) of the 20th Asian Games, pose with Ding Ning (1st L), chair of the Athletes' Committee of the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA), and Vinod Kumar Tiwari, deputy director general of the OCA, during the awarding ceremony at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Oct. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Hou Zhaokang)

item.title: China's new generation shines at Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
* China reaffirmed its continental dominance by topping the gold medal table for a record 12th straight Asian Games, securing 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals - its best-ever haul at an overseas Asiad.
* The Games signaled a changing of the guard, with 548 of China's 815 athletes making their Asiad debuts and over a quarter born in 2005 or later.
* Beyond traditional disciplines, young Chinese athletes broke new ground in skateboarding, sport climbing, surfing and BMX freestyle-sports aligned with the Olympic program's youth-oriented shift.
Players of China celebrate after winning the men's 3rd place match of Football between China and Uzbekistan at 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Toyota of Aichi Prefecture, Japan, Oct. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Jia Haocheng)
NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games came to a close Sunday, with China topping the gold medal table for the 12th consecutive edition, and finishing with 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals, its best haul at an overseas Asiad.
Beyond the medal count, the Games offered a glimpse of the next generation of Chinese athletes. Young competitors rose up across a spectrum of sports -- strengthening China's traditional powerhouses, breaking new ground in emerging disciplines and signaling ambitions that extend well beyond Nagoya.
DEPTH ON DISPLAY
China's dominance in its traditional strength events was evident throughout the Games.
Chen Yuxi of China, gold medalist of the women's 10m platform and women's synchronised 10m platform, poses for photos after diving competition at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Tokyo, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Zeguo)
Diving once again provided the clearest example. With Lian Junjie winning the men's 10m platform title, China swept all 10 diving gold medals on offer at the Games. Since making its Asiad debut in 1974, China has never missed out on a diving gold medal, and the latest title was the team's 100th diving gold in Asian Games history.
That dominance extended across the water. Chinese swimmers won 30 gold, 13 silver and 11 bronze medals, their best-ever haul at the Games. They also swept all seven relay titles for the first time, while setting five Asian records and 17 Games records.
On the track and field, China continued to turn depth into medals. The team won 17 gold, 14 silver and eight bronze medals, its best show at an Asiad held outside China since Bangkok 1998, to finish atop the athletics medal table.
Shi Junhao, Liu Guoyi, Chen Yujie and Chen Jinfeng (L to R) of team China celebrate after the 4x100m relay mixed final of Athletics at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Lui Siu Wai)
The momentum also extended to other medal-rich events. China claimed 16 of the overall 28 shooting titles and set five world records.
"The Asiad gave us an opportunity to test our preparations for Los Angeles 2028," said Wang Lian, an official with China's shooting and archery administration. "It was also an important step in developing our team, particularly our promising young athletes."
Weightlifting and gymnastics further underscored China's strength in established events. Yang Liuyue broke world records in the snatch and total in the women's 61kg category, while the men's gymnastics team captured its 13th consecutive Games title and the women's team extended its winning streak to 14 editions.
Yang Liuyue of China competes during the women's 61kg final of Weightlifting at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Yu Yang)
YOUTH TAKES FLIGHT
China's delegation had a distinctly youthful look at the Asiad. Of its 815 athletes, 548 were making their Asian Games debuts, while 27 percent were born in 2005 or later.
In the women's 400m individual medley, 13-year-old Yu Zidi and 15-year-old Ke Wenxi took gold and silver.
Yu won three golds, setting Asian Games records in the 200m butterfly and 400m individual medley, as well as an Asian record in the 200m individual medley. Her performances earned her the women's Most Valuable Player award, announced by the Olympic Council of Asia on Sunday.
They arrived with talent, but talent alone was not enough. Behind their breakthroughs were years of repetition, training and persistence.
Yu Zidi (R) and Ke Wenxi of China react after the women's 400m individual medley final at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Tokyo, Japan, Sept. 23, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Zhizun)
"Only I know how much I went through this year. But I got through it all. I hope I can keep getting better and better," Yu said.
19-year-old Zhang Zhanshuo won seven gold medals, the most of any athlete at the Games. His celebration of counting the golds on his fingers in the pool became one of the memorable images.
That confidence was on display in the field, too. 18-year-old javelin thrower Yan Ziyi made an immediate impact, launching 70.46 meters with her first attempt to improve the Games record by 4.37 meters.
Yan Ziyi of China competes during the women's javelin throw final of Athletics at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 27, 2026. (Xinhua/Luo Yuan)
"I plan to save my chance to break the world record for the 2027 World Championships in Beijing," Yan said.
The emergence of young athletes such as teenage sprinter Chen Yujie offers a glimpse of what could lie ahead for Asian athletics.
The 17-year-old competed in four events and won three golds and a silver, including a gold in the women's 100m in a Games-record 11.06 seconds.
Off the track, her confidence was just as striking. A photo that she took a nap in the athletes' lounge before the final became a hit on Chinese social media.
Chen Yujie of China celebrates after winning the women's 100m final of Athletics at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Lui Siu Wai)
"These Asian Games have given me a lot of motivation. Now that it's over, I'm already looking ahead to the next challenge," Chen said. "I hope that one day I can represent China and Asian women on the world stage and showcase our strength at the Olympics."
BREAKING NEW GROUND
Young athletes are opening up new possibilities for Chinese sports.
After years of struggling to regain the footing, China's men's football team beat Uzbekistan in a penalty shootout on Saturday to win a bronze medal, its first in 28 years at the Games. The result gave Chinese fans something more to celebrate during the National Day holiday.
"This is the most valuable medal of my career," said 21-year-old center back Peng Xiao. "But I would rather see it as a starting point. I hope the generation that comes after us can one day stand higher on the podium."
As the Olympic program embraces younger, more urban sports, skateboarding, sport climbing, surfing and BMX freestyle have become regular features at the Asian Games. Chinese athletes are making their mark in these events, chasing results while gaining recognition on the world stage.
China's climbers made their presence felt on National Day, sweeping the women's boulder and men's speed titles to claim the country's first Asian Games gold medals in Olympic events. With Olympic and world champions in the field, both victories were hard-earned.
Yang Siqi of China competes during the women's shortboard gold medal match of Surfing against Ikeda Mirai of Japan at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Tahara of Aichi Prefecture, Japan, Sept. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Haobo)
For 17-year-old Yang Siqi, reaching the Asiad surfing final and winning women's shortboard silver turned what once seemed out of reach into reality. The teenager from the mountainous region of southwestern China secured the country's first Asian Games surfing medal.
Her dedication in training even caught the attention of Song Min, a coach with South Korea's surfing team, who said he believed Yang could one day make it to the Olympics.
"I have never been afraid of surfing since I first started," Yang said. "The next step is to keep improving, one step at a time."
China's skateboarders also came out on top against the host nation Japan, taking gold and bronze in the women's street event with composed performances when it mattered most.
Sun Sibei of China competes during the women's park final of Cycling BMX Freestyle at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 27, 2026. (Xinhua/Deng Hua)
21-year-old Sun Sibei made history by winning China's first gold in the cycling BMX freestyle, which made its Asian Games debut.
"I hope this niche sport can reach a wider audience, so more people can see the twists and turns in the air, and more children can have the chance to try BMX at facilities close to home," Sun said.
The younger athletes are telling a different story, a story of confidence, exploration and willingness to step into unfamiliar territory. To some extent, these Games left behind more than medals: they opened up a new path for Chinese sport.

item.title: Flag-raising ceremony held at Tian'anmen Square to celebrate 77th founding anniversary of PRC
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-01
A flag-raising ceremony to celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China (PRC) was held at Tian'anmen Square in Beijing on Thursday.
The Guard of Honor of the Chinese People's Liberation Army escorted the national flag to the square, while the military band played the national anthem.
Many people from across China gathered at the square to watch the ceremony.

item.title: Activities held across China to celebrate National Day
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-01
Cities across China are decorating landmark sites with national flags and floral displays as National Day arrives, and people hold various activities to celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China.
